title: Pride and Prejudice: Chapter XXXVIII
enhanced_title: Pride and Prejudice: Chapter XXXVIII - The Departure from Hunsford
author: Jane Austen
description: Elizabeth Bennet bids farewell to Hunsford and the Collinses, departing with Maria Lucas after six weeks of complex social dynamics, subtle revelations, and Mr. Darcy's unexpected proposal. The chapter captures Charlotte's resigned satisfaction with her marriage, Mr. Collins's self-congratulatory farewells, and Elizabeth's anxious anticipation of revealing momentous news to Jane.

analysis_entries.paragraph: Mr. Collins's farewell speech exemplifies his characteristic blend of self-deprecation and self-congratulation. While ostensibly apologizing for the humble conditions at Hunsford, he simultaneously emphasizes the superior social connections through Lady Catherine, revealing his inability to distinguish genuine hospitality from social climbing. His mention of 'condescension' betrays his class consciousness and desire to position himself advantageously, even in the act of saying goodbye.
analysis_entries.anchor_text_end_of_sentence:
and that we have done everything in our power to prevent you spending
your time unpleasantly.

analysis_entries.paragraph: The phrase 'smiling solemnity' used to describe Mr. Collins's reply is a masterful oxymoron capturing the absurdity of his character. Austen uses this paradoxical expression to highlight how Collins attempts to balance his perpetual need for gravity with his desire to appear pleased, resulting in an awkward hybrid that Elizabeth must navigate with careful diplomacy. The phrase encapsulates in two words what the entire chapter dramatizes at length: the comic gap between Collins's self-image and the reality others perceive.
analysis_entries.anchor_text_end_of_sentence:
with a more smiling
solemnity replied,--

analysis_entries.paragraph: Collins's boast of 'superior society' and 'extraordinary advantage and blessing' in connection with Rosings reveals the central irony of the novel: genuine happiness and social elevation are rarely synonymous. His obliviousness to the actual quality of these social interactions—marked by Lady Catherine's tyranny and his own sycophancy—underscores Austen's critique of social hierarchies and false values. That he presents proximity to Rosings as compensation for every domestic deficiency exposes how thoroughly he has confused deference with dignity.
analysis_entries.anchor_text_end_of_sentence: sharers of our intimacy at Rosings.

analysis_entries.paragraph: Elizabeth's difficulty in uniting 'civility and truth' represents the perpetual challenge she faces in this social circle. Her predicament illustrates the tension between honest feeling and social obligation that runs throughout the novel. Austen presents Elizabeth as morally constrained by politeness, forced to navigate conversations where truth would be socially catastrophic.
analysis_entries.anchor_text_end_of_sentence:
Elizabeth tried to unite civility
and truth in a few short sentences.

analysis_entries.paragraph: Austen's authorial aside 'Poor Charlotte! it was melancholy to leave her to such society!' marks a rare direct intervention revealing Elizabeth's true feelings. This moment of frank sympathy contrasts sharply with the constrained dialogue, offering readers privileged insight into Elizabeth's judgment of Charlotte's marriage while acknowledging Charlotte's agency in choosing her fate. The observation that Charlotte 'did not seem to ask for compassion' further complicates the reader's response, suggesting that Charlotte's contentment, however limited, is genuine. Her home and housekeeping, parish and poultry, retain their hold on her, and Austen renders this without condescension. The passage thus holds two truths simultaneously: Elizabeth's pity is real, and Charlotte's satisfaction is real.
analysis_entries.anchor_text_end_of_sentence: had not yet lost their charms.

analysis_entries.paragraph: The comedy of Mr. Collins's sudden recollection that they had forgotten to leave messages for the ladies of Rosings perfectly captures his social anxiety and obsession with proper forms. His 'consternation' at this oversight reveals how thoroughly he has internalized the rituals of deference to Lady Catherine's family, treating social obligation with the gravity of religious duty. That this moment of panic occurs at the very threshold of departure—door nearly shut, carriage ready—underscores how completely the performance of deference governs his every action.
analysis_entries.anchor_text_end_of_sentence: forgotten to leave any message for the ladies of Rosings.

analysis_entries.paragraph: Elizabeth's private reflection 'And how much I shall have to conceal!' following Maria's innocent tally of social events creates dramatic irony and underscores the chapter's tension between surface appearances and hidden truths. This contrast between Maria's superficial accounting and Elizabeth's weighty secrets encapsulates the novel's exploration of how social events conceal rather than reveal true significance. The juxtaposition of Maria's nine dinners at Rosings against Elizabeth's unspoken knowledge of Darcy's proposal and Wickham's villainy measures the vast distance between social surface and psychological depth. The chapter closes not on departure but on interiority, reminding the reader that the most consequential events of the visit have left no visible trace.
analysis_entries.anchor_text_end_of_sentence: And how much I shall have to conceal!

quote_entries.quote: Our plain manner of living, our small rooms, and few domestics, and the little we see of the world, must make Hunsford extremely dull to a young lady like yourself; but I hope you will believe us grateful for the condescension.
